articles.title: Two astronauts who flew farther than anyone before are taking new NASA roles
articles.summary: Artemis II astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning to emeritus status at NASA after their historic journey around the Moon earlier this year. The pair will continue advising and mentoring NASA teams as preparations accelerate for Artemis III and future lunar missions. Their experience with Orion and deep-space operations could prove especially valuable as NASA works toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface.
articles.content:
NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are beginning a new chapter after their historic Artemis II journey around the Moon earlier this year. In September, both astronauts are transitioning to emeritus status at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.

The emeritus program allows highly experienced NASA personnel to remain involved with the agency by volunteering their expertise. In these specialized consulting roles, they can help train and mentor current employees while also gaining more freedom to pursue opportunities outside their previous full time positions.

Carrying Artemis II Experience Forward

"I've had the privilege of knowing Reid and Victor for years, and both exemplify the leadership, character, and commitment that define NASA at its best," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Reid commanded Artemis II after previously spending 165 days aboard the International Space Station, while Victor brought his experience as a naval aviator, test pilot, and Crew-1 astronaut to his role as pilot. Together, they took on one of the most challenging missions in human spaceflight and helped return America to the lunar environment. As Reid and Victor transition to emeritus status, I'm grateful they will continue sharing what they learned with our astronauts, flight controllers, and engineers as we prepare for Artemis III in 2027 and the missions that follow."

As Glover moves into his new role, he plans to remain involved in aerospace, leadership, and public service both within NASA and beyond the agency. A key part of that work will involve passing along his extensive knowledge of Orion and its spacecraft systems to the teams preparing for future Artemis missions.

"As I grow into this new role, NASA and spaceflight remain a meaningful part of my journey of service," said Glover. "I'm excited to keep uplifting my friends and cheering them on as they reach for the Moon. Together, we'll keep pushing boundaries and inspiring the next giant leap."

Preparing NASA for Artemis III

Wiseman will also continue sharing lessons from his spaceflight career as NASA prepares for Artemis III. That mission is planned for low Earth orbit and will test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems.

"There is no better place to work, and there are no better people to work with, than those in this agency," said Wiseman. "NASA gave me tremendous responsibility, supported me through two space missions, and my time as chief astronaut, and was always there for my family when we needed it most. I'm thrilled to continue serving future missions and programs through the emeritus program."

NASA leaders emphasized that the transition does not mark the end of Glover and Wiseman's contributions to the agency. Instead, their experience will remain available to astronauts, engineers, flight controllers, and others working on the next stages of NASA's human spaceflight program.

"Reid and Victor's commitment to exploration, steady leadership, and service to our astronaut corps and our nation have made a lasting impact," said Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. "Throughout their careers, they have each brought excellence, humility, and purpose to every role they have held at NASA. Their contributions have helped advance our mission and inspire those around them, leaving a legacy that will continue to shape the future of human spaceflight. We are immeasurably grateful for all they have given to NASA and are glad that this is not the end of their journey with the agency."

Scott Tingle, chief of the Astronaut Office at Johnson, likewise highlighted the influence the two astronauts have had on NASA's astronaut corps.

"Reid and Victor are trusted teammates whose professionalism, calm leadership, and unwavering commitment to NASA have strengthened our office and inspired everyone around them," said Scott Tingle, chief of the Astronaut Office at Johnson. "As they transition into their emeritus roles, they leave a legacy of operational excellence that will continue shaping the astronaut corps for years to come. We're grateful that they will still be part of our community, sharing their experience and insight as they begin this next chapter."

A Historic Journey Around the Moon

Glover and Wiseman were two of the four astronauts aboard Artemis II, the first crewed mission to launch on NASA's SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and carry astronauts aboard Orion around the Moon.

They flew with NASA astronaut Christina Koch and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen on the 10-day mission. The crew safely splashed down on April 10 after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel to lunar orbit. During the mission, the four astronauts ultimately traveled farther into space than anyone before them.

The experience Glover and Wiseman gained during Artemis II is expected to play an important role in NASA's preparations for Artemis III. Their knowledge will also help support the broader Artemis campaign as NASA works toward returning American astronauts to the lunar surface with Artemis IV in 2028.

articles.personality_title: Astronauts from Artemis II take new roles to guide NASA’s next Moon missions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Earlier this year, NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman flew farther into space than anyone in over 50 years on the Artemis II mission. They orbited the Moon aboard the Orion spacecraft, marking an important step in NASA’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface.

**What happened** – In September, Glover and Wiseman began new roles as emeritus astronauts at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. This status allows them to step back from full-time duties but still share their knowledge by advising and mentoring NASA teams. Their experience from Artemis II, including deep-space operations and spacecraft systems, will support preparations for the upcoming Artemis III mission.

**Impact** – This change is important because it keeps valuable expertise inside NASA while giving the astronauts freedom to explore other opportunities. Glover and Wiseman’s firsthand experience with the Orion spacecraft and lunar orbit will help train astronauts and engineers, improving the chances of success for future missions. Their leadership and lessons learned will guide NASA as it plans to land humans on the Moon again.

**What's next step** – The astronauts will continue mentoring teams as NASA prepares for Artemis III, planned for 2027, which will test spacecraft docking and other critical skills in low Earth orbit. Their involvement will also influence later missions, including Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts on the Moon.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Two astronauts who traveled farther into space than anyone recently are now sharing their experience to help NASA prepare for future Moon missions and keep human space exploration moving forward.

articles.personality_title_es: Astronautas de Artemis II asumen nuevos roles para guiar las próximas misiones lunares de la NASA
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – A principios de este año, los astronautas de la NASA Victor Glover y Reid Wiseman viajaron más lejos en el espacio que cualquier persona en más de 50 años durante la misión Artemis II. Orbitaron alrededor de la Luna a bordo de la nave Orion, un paso importante en el plan de la NASA para regresar humanos a la superficie lunar.

**Qué pasó** – En septiembre, Glover y Wiseman comenzaron nuevos roles como astronautas eméritos en el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA en Houston. Este estatus les permite reducir sus tareas a tiempo completo, pero seguir compartiendo su conocimiento al asesorar y orientar a los equipos de la NASA. Su experiencia en Artemis II, incluyendo operaciones en espacio profundo y sistemas de la nave, apoyará la preparación para la próxima misión Artemis III.

**Impacto** – Este cambio es importante porque mantiene la experiencia valiosa dentro de la NASA y da a los astronautas la libertad de explorar otras oportunidades. La experiencia directa de Glover y Wiseman con la nave Orion y la órbita lunar ayudará a entrenar a astronautas e ingenieros, mejorando las probabilidades de éxito de futuras misiones. Su liderazgo y las lecciones aprendidas guiarán a la NASA en sus planes para regresar humanos a la Luna.

**Próximo paso** – Los astronautas seguirán orientando a los equipos mientras la NASA se prepara para Artemis III, programada para 2027, que probará el acoplamiento de naves y otras habilidades clave en órbita terrestre baja. Su participación también influirá en misiones posteriores, incluyendo Artemis IV, que busca aterrizar astronautas en la Luna.

**Resumen en una frase** – Dos astronautas que viajaron más lejos en el espacio recientemente ahora comparten su experiencia para ayudar a la NASA a preparar futuras misiones lunares y avanzar en la exploración humana del espacio.
